sections.h2: Tompkinsville offices that collect and assess tax
sections.html:
Courthouse suites at 200 North Main Street in Tompkinsville hold most of the tax offices. The PVA values homes, the sheriff takes in the payment, and the county clerk looks after delinquent bills and liens. The county attorney, in a separate office on North Main Street, arranges payment plans.

This is the Monroe County in Kentucky, on the Eastern Pennyroyal Plateau.

All of these are in Tompkinsville, KY 42167.

  • Sheriff: tax collection. 200 North Main Street, Suite E, phone (270) 487-6622.
  • PVA: assessments and exemptions. 200 North Main Street, Suite A, phone (270) 487-6401.
  • County Clerk: delinquent bills and liens. 200 North Main Street, Suite D, phone (270) 487-5471.
  • County Attorney: 215 North Main Street, phone (270) 487-6303.

Before paying anyone on a late bill, ask the clerk whether your certificate has been sold, because a buyer can attach costs of its own.

Through April 15 you pay the sheriff under the calendar in KRS 134.015.

Monroe County bill by payment date
When you payWhat it costs
Through November 12 percent discount
November 2 to December 31Printed amount
JanuaryExtra 5 percent
February 1 to April 1510 percent penalty, 21 percent combined penalty on the state schedule

A bill that reaches the clerk grows further. Paying within five business days of the transfer costs less than waiting, so move quickly if you miss April 15.

Right after April 15 the clerk issues a certificate of delinquency, a lien of record against the property. That happens on or about April 16. Interest climbs monthly, so an early payment costs less.

The clerk holds a sale of unpaid certificates each fall in the clerk's office, and the clerk can tell you the date. A certificate unpaid at the sale may go to a private party who adds heavy administrative costs. The county attorney or a buyer may pursue foreclosure.

  • By mail: money orders only.
  • In person at the clerk's desk: check, cash or credit card, and card fees may apply.
  • Installments: the County Attorney's office offers them, though a sold bill no longer qualifies.

The clerk can also tell you by phone whether a certificate was bought and by whom.

Monroe covers about 329 square miles along the Tennessee border, formed in 1820. Fountain Run and Gamaliel are the other cities, and the county sits in the Upper Cumberland hills along the Cumberland River. The Old Mulkey Meetinghouse State Historic Site draws visitors.

The 2020 count of 11,338 was above the 10,963 recorded in 2010, but the mid-2025 estimate of 11,191 is 1.3 percent lower. There are 5,300 housing units. Owners live in 70.9 percent of homes, which leaves more room for rentals. A typical owner-occupied home is worth $115,900 and typical rent is $657. Owner costs run $1,056 a month with a mortgage and $397 without one. Jobs counted in 2023 came to 2,649, which is 1.9 percent below 2022.

A PVA conference comes first, and the state requires it before anyone can file. The roll opens to the public on the first Monday of May for about two weeks, and the clerk's office accepts filings through the next workday after it closes.

The filing states your own opinion of value. Should bills go out before the appeal ends and the final figure beat your claim, a supplemental bill covers the gap. The board meets between 25 and 35 days after the window and may sit five days. Bring evidence: land and building details, insurance policies, construction costs and sales listings.

Across 329 square miles and 34.4 people per square mile, many Monroe County sales come with land. The PVA must visit every parcel at least every four years and add new construction yearly. Farm land may be assessed at agricultural value instead of fair cash value, so ask the PVA how your acreage is classified before you list it.

Parcels near the Tennessee line, along the river or up in the hills can differ widely. If the roll shows a building that was torn down, or misses a barn you added, raise it at a PVA conference.

Anyone who owns and lives in a house and has turned 65, or carries a total disability classification, may claim it. Apply at the Monroe County PVA with proof, on the state's form.

KRS 132.810 sets one exemption per unit, even if the owner is both elderly and disabled, or several older residents share the unit. The amount follows a federal price index and is rechecked every two years. Report a sale or the owner's death to the PVA.

sections.h2: Selling a house that owes tax
sections.html:
It can be done, and the usual route starts with a written payoff. The sheriff supplies it before April 15, and the clerk does afterward, when the figure rises monthly and carries the clerk and attorney fees.

Under KRS 134.015 the person who owned on January 1 owes that year's tax personally, and a lien can follow the property for 11 years. Houses in Monroe County that need work, or came to heirs, can change hands with a bill still open, so build the payoff into your numbers when you compare a listing with a cash sale.

Gather your deed, your last bill and any exemption approval before you start. Ask the PVA to confirm the parcel details, since acreage and outbuildings are common sources of mismatch. If the owner has died, bring the papers that show who may sign. After closing, tell the PVA the new owner's name so the next bill is mailed correctly and the old exemption ends. A cash buyer can often close without repairs, which helps when a roof or other work would stall a lender.

Start by calling the sheriff for the current balance and, if April 15 has gone by, the clerk, since the bill will have moved there. Ask whether a certificate exists on the parcel and whether any buyer holds it. If one does, the payoff includes that buyer's costs, so get the figure in writing and dated close to closing.

Next, decide in the sales contract who pays the year's tax, because the January 1 owner is the one billed. The closing agent then pays the tax out of the sale money and the clerk records the new deed. A buyer who plans a conventional loan will usually want the tax cleared first, while a cash buyer can close around it.

Monroe County has a mix of town lots in Tompkinsville, small-town homes in Fountain Run and Gamaliel, and rural tracts. A town lot rarely needs more than a payoff and a clear deed. A tract with acreage may also need the PVA to confirm its classification and boundaries before a buyer will commit.

faqs.q: Who accepts Monroe County property tax payments?
faqs.a: The county sheriff, in Suite E at 200 North Main Street, Tompkinsville. Call (270) 487-6622.

faqs.q: When is the Monroe County tax sale?
faqs.a: The clerk holds a sale of unpaid certificates each fall. Phone (270) 487-5471 to learn the date and whether a certificate was sold.

faqs.q: Is an installment plan available on a late Monroe County bill?
faqs.a: Yes, through the County Attorney's office, provided the certificate was not sold at the tax sale.

faqs.q: Can a delinquent bill be paid to the clerk by check in the mail?
faqs.a: No, mailed payments must be money orders. Checks, cash and credit cards work only at the clerk's office.

faqs.q: Where is the Monroe County PVA?
faqs.a: Suite A, 200 North Main Street, Tompkinsville. The office phone is (270) 487-6401.
